extracted.intended_audience: students, writers, and instructors seeking concise rules of English usage and composition
extracted.subtask_description: Concise prescriptive rules and principles for writing plain, effective English: punctuation and usage rules plus principles of composition for sentence and paragraph-level clarity and vigor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form the possessive singular of nouns by adding 's.
rubrics_metrics.description: Follow this rule whatever the final consonant. Thus write Charles's friend; Burns's poems; the witch's malice. The pronominal possessives hers, its, theirs, yours, and oneself have no apostrophe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exceptions: the possessive of ancient proper names in -es and -is, the possessive Jesus', and set phrases such as for conscience' sake, for righteousness' sake. Common alternatives replace forms like Achilles' heel with the heel of Achilles. Usage noted as that of the U.S. Government Printing Office and Oxford University Press. Examples: Charles's friend; Burns's poems; the witch's malice.

rubrics_metrics.name: In a series of three or more terms with a single conjunction, use a comma after each term except the last.
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a comma after each term in a series of three or more when there is a single conjunction before the last term.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: red, white, and blue; gold, silver, or copper; He opened the letter, read it, and made a note of its contents. Note: in the names of business firms the last comma is omitted (e.g., Brown, Shipley & Co.). Usage endorsed by Government Printing Office and Oxford University Press.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enclose parenthetic expressions between commas.
rubrics_metrics.description: Parenthetic expressions should be enclosed between commas (or between comma and period at sentence end). If the interruption is slight, commas may be omitted, but never insert one comma and omit the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Difficult to apply in borderline cases (e.g., single words like however). Never set off independent clauses by commas (see Rule 5). If a parenthetic expression is preceded by a conjunction, place the first comma before the conjunction. Always parenthetic (and to be enclosed by commas): (1) the year when part of a date and day of month when following day of week (e.g., April 6, 1917; Monday, November 11, 1918); (2) abbreviations etc. and jr.; (3) non-restrictive relative clauses (which add supplementary information) and similar clauses introduced by conjunctions of time or place. Contrast with restrictive clauses (no commas) that identify the antecedent. Also covers setting off phrases or dependent clauses preceding or following the main clause (examples throughout Rules 4–7, 16, 18). Examples of indefensible punctuation: Marjorie's husband, Colonel Nelson paid us a visit yesterday. My brother you will be pleased to hear, is now in perfect health.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place a comma before a conjunction introducing a co-ordinate clause.
rubrics_metrics.description: Place a comma before a conjunction (and, but, or, nor, for, so, yet, as when co-ordinating) that introduces a second independent clause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: The early records of the city have disappeared, and the story of its first years can no longer be reconstructed. Two-part sentences with as (because), for, or, nor, while likewise require a comma. If the second member is introduced by an adverb (accordingly, therefore, then, thus, etc.) and not a conjunction, use a semicolon (see Rule 5). Uses of so and yet can be conjunctional or adverbial; choose punctuation accordingly. If a dependent clause or introductory phrase precedes the second independent clause, no comma is needed after the conjunction. When the subject is the same and expressed only once, use a comma if the connective is but; omit the comma if the connective is and and the relation is close: e.g., I have heard his arguments, but am still unconvinced. He has had several years' experience and is thoroughly competent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not join independent clauses by a comma.
rubrics_metrics.description: If two clauses are grammatically complete and not joined by a conjunction, separate them with a semicolon rather than a comma.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Stevenson's romances are entertaining; they are full of exciting adventures. It is nearly half past five; we cannot reach town before dark. It is also correct to use two sentences (periods). If a conjunction is inserted, use a comma (see Rule 4). Note that when the second clause begins with an adverb (accordingly, besides, then, therefore, thus) and no conjunction, a semicolon is required. Exceptions: very short clauses alike in form may permit a comma (Man proposes, God disposes). Colloquial comma usage (I hardly knew him, he was so changed) occurs in speech and dialogue but is inappropriate in formal writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not break sentences in two.
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use a period where a comma should be; avoid splitting what should be a single sentence into sentences improperly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of incorrect splitting: I met them on a Cunard liner several years ago. Coming home from Liverpool to New York. He was an interesting talker. A man who had traveled all over the world and lived in half a dozen countries. Replace the period with a comma and continue. Exception: permissible emphatic fragments (Again and again he called out. No reply.) but only when emphasis is clearly warranted and not a punctuation/syntax error.

rubrics_metrics.name: A participial phrase at the beginning of a sentence must refer to the grammatical subject.
rubrics_metrics.description: A participial phrase that begins a sentence must grammatically modify the sentence's subject; otherwise the sentence is misformed or ludicrous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorrect: Walking slowly down the road, he saw a woman accompanied by two children. (walking refers to he, not the woman). To make walking refer to the woman, recast: He saw a woman accompanied by two children, walking slowly down the road. Other initial modifiers (participial phrases preceded by conjunctions/prepositions, nouns in apposition, adjectives/adjective phrases) follow the same rule. Examples and correct recastings provided: On arriving in Chicago, his friends met him at the station → When he arrived (or On his arrival) in Chicago, his friends met him at the station. A soldier of proved valor, they entrusted him with the defence of the city → A soldier of proved valor, he was entrusted with the defence of the city. Sentences violating this rule are often ludicrous (Being in a dilapidated condition, I was able to buy the house very cheap.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Make the paragraph the unit of composition: one paragraph to each topic.
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat each topic as a separate paragraph; the paragraph is the unit of composition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a subject is slight or treated briefly, a single paragraph may suffice. Ordinarily subdivide into topics with one paragraph per topic to aid the reader—the paragraph signals a new step. The degree of subdivision varies with length; examples are given for short notices, reports on poems (sections A–G), novel discussions (Setting, Plot, Characters, Purpose), and historical events (what led up, account, consequences). Single-sentence paragraphs should ordinarily be avoided except for transitions or in dialogue (each speech starts a new paragraph). After writing a paragraph, examine whether subdivision improves it; avoid many single-sentence paragraphs unless for special effect or in textbooks/guidebooks.

rubrics_metrics.name: As a rule, begin each paragraph with a topic sentence; end it in conformity with the beginning.
rubrics_metrics.description: Start paragraphs with a topic sentence and have following sentences develop, explain, or support it; end by emphasizing or drawing consequence from that topic sentence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommended paragraph structure: (a) topic sentence near beginning; (b) succeeding sentences explain/establish/develop the topic sentence; (c) final sentence emphasizes the topic or states an important consequence. Avoid ending with digressions or unimportant detail. Transitional sentences or phrases may precede the topic sentence; if many are needed, set them as a separate paragraph. Ways to relate body to topic sentence: restatement, definition, denial of contrary, illustrations, proofs, implications. Examples with annotated paragraphs (Stevenson, Lecky) illustrate the method. In narration/description, opening may be a concise comprehensive statement followed by details; brief narrative paragraphs often lack formal topic sentences and serve as rhetorical pauses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the active voice.
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer the active voice because it is more direct, vigorous, and concise than passive constructions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: I shall always remember my first visit to Boston (active) vs My first visit to Boston will always be remembered by me (passive, less direct). Passive is sometimes convenient or necessary (The dramatists of the Restoration are little esteemed to-day). Choose voice to make the intended subject prominent. Avoid making one passive depend directly on another (e.g., Gold was not allowed to be exported → It was forbidden to export gold / The export of gold was prohibited). Avoid using a noun expressing the whole action as the subject with a perfunctory passive verb (A survey of this region was made in 1900 → This region was surveyed in 1900). Active voice often strengthens tame sentences by substituting vivid verbs for weak expressions (There were a great number of dead leaves lying on the ground → Dead leaves covered the ground).

rubrics_metrics.name: Put statements in positive form.
rubrics_metrics.description: Make definite assertions; avoid hedging, evasive negatives, and non-committal language. Use not only to deny but not as evasion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer affirmative phrasing over negatives: He was not very often on time → He usually came late. He did not think that studying Latin was much use → He thought the study of Latin useless. Replace weak negative constructions with direct adjectives or verbs (not honest → dishonest; did not remember → forgot; did not pay any attention to → ignored). Use negative-positive antithesis for emphasis (Not charity, but simple justice). Note negative words other than not can be strong: The sun never sets upon the British flag.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use definite, specific, concrete language.
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer specific to general, definite to vague, and concrete to abstract to arouse and hold reader attention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: A period of unfavorable weather set in → It rained every day for a week. He showed satisfaction as he took possession of his well-earned reward → He grinned as he pocketed the coin. Provide particular instances when discussing general principles. Quoted theory (Herbert Spencer) explains superiority of specific expressions because readers think in particulars. Literary examples (Homer, Dante, Shakespeare, Browning) show vividness achieved by definite details. In exposition and argument, do not lose hold on concrete—give significant, vivid details rather than vague generalities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Omit needless words.
rubrics_metrics.description: Vigorous writing is concise; sentences and paragraphs should contain no unnecessary words or sentences—make every word tell.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify and remove redundant or wordy common expressions: the question as to whether → whether; there is no doubt but that → no doubt/doubtless; used for fuel purposes → used for fuel; he is a man who → he; in a hasty manner → hastily; this is a subject which → this subject. Particularly eliminate the fact that (owing to the fact that → since; in spite of the fact that → though; call your attention to the fact that → remind you). Who is / which was etc. often superfluous: His brother, who is a member of the same firm → His brother, a member of the same firm. Examples show combining several sentences into one concise sentence reduces wordiness and improves force. Many examples of compressing paragraphs and sentences are provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid a succession of loose sentences
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid constructing paragraphs as a series of loose sentences consisting of two coordinate clauses with the second introduced by a conjunction or relative (and, but, so, who, which, when, where, while used non-restrictively), because a succession becomes monotonous and tedious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An unskilful writer may produce a whole paragraph of such sentences, leading to triteness and weakness. The book gives an example paragraph composed of many such sentences and calls it weak apart from its emptiness due to the structural monotony. Vary sentence structure, avoid repeated loose constructions, and use other sentence forms to maintain reader interest (see Rule 4 and Rule 14 discussion).
